Social Media Engagement Analytics

What drives likes, comments, shares and views across six platforms?

Himaja Vuchuru

14 October 2026

Executive summary

This report analyses 5,000 social-media posts across six platforms (Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, LinkedIn) published across 2024–2025, and asks a simple business question: what actually drives engagement? The headline patterns are then independently replicated on a second, genuinely real dataset — the UCI Facebook Metrics dataset of 500 real posts (Moro et al., 2016).

Key findings:

  • Platform is the dominant lever — but in two different ways. TikTok wins on raw engagement volume (about 5× Instagram, holding everything else constant), whereas Instagram is the most efficient platform, converting a higher share of each view into an interaction.
  • Reach drives engagement volume. Likes, comments, shares and saves rise together with views, so getting seen is the first-order lever (Spearman \(\rho \approx 0.65\) between reach and interactions — see the real-data replication in §7).
  • Engagement rate is strongly right-skewed: the typical post sits near 2% of followers, but a small number of viral posts reach into the hundreds or thousands of percent.
  • Content format influences volume, not efficiency. Once platform is controlled, format and category have little effect on how efficiently a view is converted; the platform × format interaction is not statistically significant.
  • The results are robust. Two independent checks — 5-fold cross-validation and re-fitting after removing 295 data-quality anomalies — leave every conclusion intact.
  • Real data agrees. On the independent UCI Facebook dataset, post type and posting month are again significant drivers of engagement, reproducing the core story.

1. Introduction and objectives

Social-media managers must decide what to post, where, and when. This project builds a reproducible R pipeline that (i) cleans post-level analytics, (ii) explores engagement patterns with ggplot2, and (iii) quantifies the drivers of engagement with regression, before (iv) replicating the findings on an external, peer-reviewed dataset.

Research questions

  1. How does engagement vary by content type, platform and posting period?
  2. How are views, likes, comments and shares related to one another?
  3. Which account, content and timing features best predict an engagement measure, and how much of the variation can we explain?
  4. Do the findings generalise to real, externally collected data?

2. Dataset description and source

2.1 Primary dataset

  • Dataset: Social Media Engagement Dataset (URL: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/aviral342/social-media-engagement-dataset).
  • Coverage: 5,000 posts, 6 platforms, 12 content categories, Jan 2024 – Dec 2025.
  • Granularity: one row per post.
  • Licence: public Kaggle dataset, re-downloadable via the kagglehub client.
  • Note on provenance: the Kaggle publisher states the engagement figures are platform-realistic and generated for educational/research use. To guard against over-claiming from a single synthetic source, this project also validates its conclusions on real data (§2.2, §7).

2.2 Replication dataset (real, peer-reviewed)

  • Dataset: Facebook Metrics (UCI Machine Learning Repository).
  • Source: Moro, S., Rita, P., & Vala, B. (2016). Predicting social media performance metrics and the impact of the type of content: A case study in the banking sector. Journal of Business Research, 69(9).
  • Coverage: 500 posts from a cosmetics brand’s Facebook page, 2014.
  • Why it matters: it is real, externally published data, so agreement between the two datasets strengthens the credibility of the methodology and the findings.

The raw files are stored at data/raw/social_media_engagement.csv and data/raw/facebook_metrics.csv (provenance in data/raw/SOURCES.md).

Variable (primary) Role Description
Timestamp time Date and time the post was published
Platform factor Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, LinkedIn
Content_Type factor Platform-native format (Reel, Short, Tweet, Article, …)
Category factor Content topic (Business, Fitness, Travel, …)
Views numeric Times the post was displayed (impressions)
Likes / Comments / Shares / Saves numeric Engagement actions
Follower_Count numeric Account size at posting time
Engagement_Rate numeric Supplied rate metric (validated in §4)
Hashtag_Count, Content_Length numeric Caption characteristics
Sentiment, Influencer_Tier, Has_Media, Is_Verified factors Account/content attributes

3. Methodology

The analysis is organised as scripts under R/, all sourced by this report:

Script Purpose
R/01_preprocess.R Load, audit and clean the data
R/02_eda.R Summary statistics and eight ggplot2 visualisations
R/03_modeling.R Regression models, interaction test, cross-validation, robustness
R/04_replication.R Independent replication on the real UCI dataset

Packages: tidyverse (dplyr, tidyr, readr, stringr, forcats), lubridate, ggplot2, scales, broom, patchwork.

4. Data cleaning and preprocessing

The raw file is already tidy (one row per post), so cleaning focuses on type coercion, feature engineering and an integrity audit.

raw_path <- file.path(DIR_RAW, "social_media_engagement.csv")
raw_data <- readr::read_csv(
  raw_path,
  show_col_types = FALSE,
  col_types = readr::cols(Timestamp = readr::col_character())
)

n_raw      <- nrow(raw_data)
n_raw_cols <- ncol(raw_data)
n_missing_raw <- sum(is.na(raw_data))

Timestamps are parsed to a real datetime; the stored Hour_of_Day and Day_of_Week are then checked against it as an internal-consistency test.

# Parse the text timestamp once into a real datetime. All 5,000 values share the
# "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS" layout, so parsing succeeds for every row.
ts_parsed   <- suppressWarnings(lubridate::ymd_hms(raw_data$Timestamp, quiet = TRUE))
n_bad_ts    <- sum(is.na(ts_parsed))

clean_data <- raw_data %>%
  mutate(
    Post_Timestamp = ts_parsed,
    Has_Media      = as.logical(Has_Media),
    Is_Verified    = as.logical(Is_Verified)
  )

# Internal consistency: the stored hour and weekday must agree with the datetime.
n_hour_mismatch <- sum(lubridate::hour(clean_data$Post_Timestamp) != clean_data$Hour_of_Day)
n_day_mismatch  <- sum(
  as.character(lubridate::wday(clean_data$Post_Timestamp, label = TRUE,
                               abbr = FALSE, week_start = 1)) != clean_data$Day_of_Week
)

Several derived features make the data analysis-ready: a harmonised content format, calendar fields, a posting period, a weekend flag, and two engagement metrics.

# Harmonise the platform-specific content labels (Reel / Short / Duet ... are all
# video-like) into four comparable content "formats".
format_lookup <- c(
  Video = "Video", Reel = "Video", Short = "Video", Live = "Video",
  Photo = "Image", Carousel = "Image", Story = "Image",
  Duet  = "Interactive", Stitch = "Interactive", Poll = "Interactive",
  Post  = "Text/Article", Tweet = "Text/Article", Thread = "Text/Article",
  Article = "Text/Article", Document = "Text/Article",
  `Community Post` = "Text/Article", Retweet = "Text/Article"
)

clean_data <- clean_data %>%
  mutate(
    Content_Format = unname(format_lookup[Content_Type]),
    Date           = lubridate::as_date(Post_Timestamp),
    Year           = lubridate::year(Post_Timestamp),
    Month          = lubridate::month(Post_Timestamp, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE),
    Year_Month     = lubridate::floor_date(Post_Timestamp, "month"),
    Weekday        = lubridate::wday(Post_Timestamp, label = TRUE,
                                     abbr = FALSE, week_start = 1),
    Hour           = lubridate::hour(Post_Timestamp),
    Posting_Period = case_when(
      Hour >= 5  & Hour < 12 ~ "Morning",
      Hour >= 12 & Hour < 17 ~ "Afternoon",
      Hour >= 17 & Hour < 22 ~ "Evening",
      TRUE                   ~ "Night"
    ),
    Is_Weekend       = Weekday %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday"),
    # Volume of engagement (all interaction types)
    Total_Engagement = Likes + Comments + Shares + Saves,
    # Rate metric -- matches the supplied Engagement_Rate column (see validation)
    ER_by_Followers  = 100 * (Likes + Comments + Shares) / Follower_Count,
    ER_by_Views      = 100 * Total_Engagement / Views,
    # Data-quality flag: a post cannot be liked more often than it is seen
    Reaches_Viewers  = Views >= Total_Engagement
  )
# Store factors with explicit levels so ordering survives the CSV round-trip.
clean_data <- clean_data %>%
  mutate(
    Platform        = factor(Platform, levels = names(PAL_PLATFORM)),
    Content_Format  = factor(Content_Format, levels = names(PAL_FORMAT)),
    Posting_Period  = factor(Posting_Period,
                             levels = c("Morning", "Afternoon", "Evening", "Night")),
    Influencer_Tier = factor(Influencer_Tier, levels = names(PAL_TIER)),
    Sentiment       = factor(Sentiment, levels = c("Negative", "Neutral", "Positive")),
    Weekday         = factor(Weekday,
                             levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
                                        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")),
    Has_Media       = factor(Has_Media,   levels = c(TRUE, FALSE),
                             labels = c("With media", "Without media")),
    Is_Verified     = factor(Is_Verified, levels = c(TRUE, FALSE),
                             labels = c("Verified", "Not verified"))
  )

The supplied Engagement_Rate is not taken on trust: it is re-derived from the raw counts and compared. It equals 100 * (Likes + Comments + Shares) / Follower_Count.

# Confirm how the supplied Engagement_Rate is defined, so we can trust/repurpose
# it. It equals 100 * (Likes + Comments + Shares) / Follower_Count.
rate_abs_diff <- abs(clean_data$Engagement_Rate - clean_data$ER_by_Followers)
max_rate_diff <- max(rate_abs_diff, na.rm = TRUE)

Finally we log the audit trail and write the analysis-ready table. Note the 295 posts flagged where total engagement exceeds views — an artefact of the data-generation process; they are retained but flagged and their effect is examined in §6.4.

n_dup_id      <- sum(duplicated(clean_data$Post_ID))
n_missing     <- sum(is.na(clean_data))
n_views_lt_eq <- sum(!clean_data$Reaches_Viewers)

cleaning_log <- c(
  sprintf("Raw file: %s", basename(raw_path)),
  sprintf("Raw dimensions: %d rows x %d columns", n_raw, n_raw_cols),
  sprintf("Missing values in raw file: %d", n_missing_raw),
  sprintf("Duplicate Post_IDs: %d", n_dup_id),
  sprintf("Timestamps that failed to parse: %d", n_bad_ts),
  sprintf("Timestamp vs Hour_of_Day mismatches: %d", n_hour_mismatch),
  sprintf("Timestamp vs Day_of_Week mismatches: %d", n_day_mismatch),
  sprintf("Engagement_Rate == 100*(Likes+Comments+Shares)/Follower_Count (max abs diff = %.4g)",
          max_rate_diff),
  sprintf("Content labels harmonised into %d formats: %s",
          n_distinct(clean_data$Content_Format),
          paste(levels(factor(clean_data$Content_Format)), collapse = ", ")),
  sprintf("Posts flagged Views < total engagement (retained, flagged): %d",
          n_views_lt_eq),
  sprintf("Missing values after cleaning: %d", n_missing),
  sprintf("Final dimensions: %d rows x %d columns",
          nrow(clean_data), ncol(clean_data)),
  sprintf("Date range: %s to %s", min(clean_data$Date), max(clean_data$Date))
)

writeLines(cleaning_log, file.path(DIR_PROC, "cleaning_log.txt"))
cat(paste(cleaning_log, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
## Raw file: social_media_engagement.csv
## Raw dimensions: 5000 rows x 20 columns
## Missing values in raw file: 0
## Duplicate Post_IDs: 0
## Timestamps that failed to parse: 0
## Timestamp vs Hour_of_Day mismatches: 0
## Timestamp vs Day_of_Week mismatches: 0
## Engagement_Rate == 100*(Likes+Comments+Shares)/Follower_Count (max abs diff = 0.004999)
## Content labels harmonised into 4 formats: Video, Image, Interactive, Text/Article
## Posts flagged Views < total engagement (retained, flagged): 295
## Missing values after cleaning: 0
## Final dimensions: 5000 rows x 34 columns
## Date range: 2024-01-01 to 2025-12-31
readr::write_csv(clean_data, file.path(DIR_PROC, "engagement_clean.csv"))
cat(sprintf("\n[01_preprocess] Clean data written to %s\n",
            file.path(DIR_PROC, "engagement_clean.csv")))

## [01_preprocess] Clean data written to H:\Temp\opencode\social-media-engagement-analytics/data/processed/engagement_clean.csv

5. Exploratory data analysis

We now reload the cleaned table (with factor levels restored) and summarise it.

eda <- readr::read_csv(file.path(DIR_PROC, "engagement_clean.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  relevel_analysis()

5.1 Overview and summary statistics

overview <- tibble::tibble(
  Metric = c("Posts analysed", "Platforms", "Content formats",
             "Content categories", "Date range", "Total likes",
             "Total comments", "Total shares", "Total saves"),
  Value = c(format(nrow(eda), big.mark = ","),
            as.character(n_distinct(eda$Platform)),
            as.character(n_distinct(eda$Content_Format)),
            as.character(n_distinct(eda$Category)),
            paste(min(eda$Date), "to", max(eda$Date)),
            format(sum(eda$Likes), big.mark = ","),
            format(sum(eda$Comments), big.mark = ","),
            format(sum(eda$Shares), big.mark = ","),
            format(sum(eda$Saves), big.mark = ","))
)

numeric_vars <- c("Likes", "Comments", "Shares", "Saves", "Views",
                  "Follower_Count", "Total_Engagement",
                  "Engagement_Rate", "Hashtag_Count", "Content_Length")

summary_stats <- eda %>%
  select(all_of(numeric_vars)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean   = mean(value),
    Median = median(value),
    SD     = sd(value),
    Min    = min(value),
    Q1     = quantile(value, .25),
    Q3     = quantile(value, .75),
    Max    = max(value),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

platform_summary <- eda %>%
  group_by(Platform) %>%
  summarise(
    Posts        = n(),
    Median_Likes = median(Likes),
    Median_Views = median(Views),
    Mean_ER      = round(mean(Engagement_Rate), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Mean_ER))

format_summary <- eda %>%
  group_by(Content_Format) %>%
  summarise(
    Posts    = n(),
    Mean_ER  = round(mean(Engagement_Rate), 2),
    Median_ER = round(median(Engagement_Rate), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Mean_ER))

eda_text <- c(
  "==== OVERVIEW ====",
  capture.output(print(overview)),
  "",
  "==== SUMMARY STATISTICS ====",
  capture.output(print(summary_stats)),
  "",
  "==== ENGAGEMENT BY PLATFORM ====",
  capture.output(print(platform_summary)),
  "",
  "==== ENGAGEMENT BY CONTENT FORMAT ====",
  capture.output(print(format_summary)),
  "",
  sprintf("Overall mean engagement rate (by followers): %.2f%%", mean(eda$Engagement_Rate)),
  sprintf("Overall median engagement rate (by followers): %.2f%%", median(eda$Engagement_Rate)),
  sprintf("Skewness of Total_Engagement: %.2f", {
    z <- (eda$Total_Engagement - mean(eda$Total_Engagement)) / sd(eda$Total_Engagement)
    mean(z^3)
  })
)
writeLines(eda_text, file.path(DIR_PROC, "eda_summary.txt"))
cat(paste(eda_text, collapse = "\n"), "\n")

The correlation matrix already answers research question 2: the engagement actions are positively and moderately correlated (log-scale Spearman \(\rho\) between 0.23 and 0.50), with views–shares and likes–saves especially linked. Follower count and hashtag count are close to uncorrelated with the engagement actions, and longer captions correlate weakly negatively with engagement.

5.2 Engagement over time

trend_df <- eda %>%
  group_by(Year_Month = as.Date(Year_Month)) %>%
  summarise(Mean_ER = mean(Engagement_Rate), .groups = "drop")

peak <- trend_df %>% slice_max(Mean_ER, n = 1)

fig_trend <- ggplot(trend_df, aes(Year_Month, Mean_ER)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2166AC", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2166AC", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.6, se = FALSE,
              colour = "#B2182B", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(trend_df$Mean_ER), colour = "grey50",
             linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("label", x = peak$Year_Month, y = peak$Mean_ER,
           label = paste0("Peak: ", format(peak$Year_Month, "%b %Y"),
                          "\n", round(peak$Mean_ER, 1), "%"),
           hjust = 0.5, vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4, fill = "#FFF3CD") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b\n%Y", date_breaks = "3 months") +
  labs(
    title = "Engagement held steady through 2024-2025",
    subtitle = "Monthly mean engagement rate (interactions per follower) across all 5,000 posts",
    x = NULL, y = "Mean engagement rate (%)",
    caption = "Dashed red = LOESS trend; dotted grey = overall mean."
  )
save_plot(fig_trend, "fig01_trend_engagement_over_time", width = 10, height = 5.5)
print(fig_trend)

Figure 1. Monthly mean engagement rate with a LOESS trend. Engagement is remarkably stable across the two years, with no strong seasonality.

5.3 Distribution of engagement

med_log <- median(log10(eda$Engagement_Rate))
mean_log <- mean(log10(eda$Engagement_Rate))

fig_dist <- ggplot(eda, aes(log10(Engagement_Rate))) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40,
                 fill = "#4477AA", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_density(colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = med_log, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20") +
  annotate("label", x = med_log, y = Inf,
           label = paste0("median = ", round(10^med_log, 2), "%"),
           vjust = 1.4, hjust = -0.05, size = 3.3, fill = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = log10(c(0.05, 0.5, 2, 10, 50, 500, 3500)),
    labels = c("0.05%", "0.5%", "2%", "10%", "50%", "500%", "3500%")) +
  labs(
    title = "Engagement rate is strongly right-skewed",
    subtitle = "Most posts sit near 2%, but a long tail of viral posts reaches into the thousands",
    x = "Engagement rate (interactions / followers, log scale)",
    y = "Density",
    caption = "Histogram of log10(engagement rate); red curve = kernel density."
  )
save_plot(fig_dist, "fig02_distribution_engagement_rate")
print(fig_dist)

Figure 2. The engagement rate is strongly right-skewed — most posts cluster near 2%, with a long viral tail. This justifies the log transforms used throughout.

5.4 Comparison by content type and platform

fig_format <- eda %>%
  mutate(Content_Format = fct_reorder(Content_Format, Engagement_Rate, median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(Content_Format, Engagement_Rate, fill = Content_Format)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.85, width = 0.65) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.08, size = 0.7, colour = "grey20") +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3,
               fill = "white", colour = "grey10") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 12)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = PAL_FORMAT, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    title = "Video posts draw the strongest engagement",
    subtitle = "Boxes ordered by median; white diamonds mark medians (outliers hidden)",
    x = NULL, y = "Engagement rate (%)",
    caption = "Y-axis zoomed to 0-12% with coord_cartesian(); values above are clipped for readability."
  )
save_plot(fig_format, "fig03_comparison_engagement_by_content")
print(fig_format)

Figure 3. Video posts have the highest median engagement rate, text/article posts the lowest. The y-axis is zoomed with coord_cartesian() so the boxes are readable.

platform_plot <- eda %>%
  group_by(Platform) %>%
  summarise(Mean_ER = mean(Engagement_Rate),
            SE = sd(Engagement_Rate) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop")

fig_platform <- ggplot(platform_plot, aes(fct_reorder(Platform, Mean_ER), Mean_ER,
                                          fill = Platform)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.9, width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Mean_ER - SE, ymax = Mean_ER + SE),
                width = 0.2, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = PAL_PLATFORM, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    title = "Average engagement rate differs sharply by platform",
    subtitle = "Bars show mean engagement rate; whiskers show +/- 1 standard error",
    x = NULL, y = "Mean engagement rate (%)",
    caption = "Mean is sensitive to viral outliers -- medians are compared in fig03 and fig08."
  )
save_plot(fig_platform, "fig04_comparison_engagement_by_platform")
print(fig_platform)

Figure 4. Mean engagement rate by platform. TikTok leads by a wide margin; LinkedIn trails. The large means (and wide error bars) reflect viral outliers — hence the median-based views below.

6. Statistical modelling

We fit log-linear models, because the outcome variables are heavily right-skewed. Because the outcome is in \(\log_{10}\), a coefficient of \(\beta\) corresponds to a \((10^{\beta}-1)\times 100\%\) change.

  • Model A — engagement volume: \(\log_{10}(\text{Total Engagement})\) (likes + comments + shares + saves).
  • Model B — engagement efficiency: \(\log_{10}(\text{interactions per view})\).

Why not the supplied per-follower rate? The supplied Engagement_Rate has followers in its denominator and follower count is a natural predictor, which creates a circular relationship that inflates the fit. We instead measure efficiency as interactions per view, which does not share the follower term with any predictor, giving an honest estimate.

Predictors in both: \(\log_{10}\)(followers), platform, content format, category, posting period, weekend flag, sentiment, hashtag count, \(\log_{10}\)(content length) and verification status.

model_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(DIR_PROC, "engagement_clean.csv"),
                            show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  relevel_analysis() %>%
  mutate(
    log_engagement = log10(Total_Engagement),
    log_er_view    = log10(ER_by_Views)          # efficiency: interactions per view
  )

# --- Overall model formula (shared by A and the interaction model) -----------
fml_a <- log_engagement ~ log10(Follower_Count) + Platform + Content_Format +
  Category + Posting_Period + Is_Weekend + Sentiment +
  Hashtag_Count + log10(Content_Length) + Is_Verified

# --- Manual variance-inflation factors (no 'car' dependency) -----------------
vif_manual <- function(model) {
  X <- model.matrix(model)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
  v <- vapply(seq_len(ncol(X)), function(j) {
    r2 <- summary(stats::lm(X[, j] ~ X[, -j, drop = FALSE]))$r.squared
    1 / (1 - r2)
  }, numeric(1))
  tibble::tibble(term = colnames(X), VIF = round(v, 2))
}

# --- 5-fold cross-validation RMSE --------------------------------------------
cv_rmse <- function(form, data, response, k = 5, seed = 123) {
  set.seed(seed)
  folds <- sample(rep(seq_len(k), length.out = nrow(data)))
  fold_err <- vapply(seq_len(k), function(i) {
    tr <- data[folds != i, ]
    te <- data[folds == i, ]
    m  <- stats::lm(form, data = tr)
    sqrt(mean((te[[response]] - stats::predict(m, newdata = te))^2))
  }, numeric(1))
  mean(fold_err)
}
model_a <- lm(fml_a, data = model_df)
glance_a <- broom::glance(model_a)
tidy_a   <- broom::tidy(model_a, conf.int = TRUE)
vif_a    <- vif_manual(model_a)

cat("==== MODEL A: log10(Total Engagement) ====\n")
## ==== MODEL A: log10(Total Engagement) ====
print(glance_a)
## # A tibble: 1 × 12
##   r.squared adj.r.squared sigma statistic p.value    df logLik   AIC   BIC
##       <dbl>         <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1     0.686         0.684 0.244      374.       0    29  -23.6  109.  311.
## # ℹ 3 more variables: deviance <dbl>, df.residual <int>, nobs <int>
std_df <- model_df %>%
  mutate(across(c(Total_Engagement, Follower_Count, Content_Length),
                ~ as.numeric(scale(log10(.x + 1))), .names = "z_{.col}"))
model_std <- lm(z_Total_Engagement ~ z_Follower_Count + Platform + Content_Format +
                  Category + Posting_Period + Is_Weekend + Sentiment +
                  Hashtag_Count + z_Content_Length + Is_Verified, data = std_df)
cat("\nStrongest standardised predictors (Model A):\n")
## 
## Strongest standardised predictors (Model A):
print(broom::tidy(model_std) %>% filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
        arrange(desc(abs(estimate))) %>% slice_head(n = 8) %>%
        mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))))
## # A tibble: 8 × 5

# Efficiency metric = interactions per view. Follower count does NOT appear in

model_b <- lm(log_er_view ~ log10(Follower_Count) + Platform + Content_Format +
                Category + Posting_Period + Is_Weekend + Sentiment +
                Hashtag_Count + log10(Content_Length) + Is_Verified,
              data = model_df)
glance_b <- broom::glance(model_b)
tidy_b   <- broom::tidy(model_b, conf.int = TRUE)

cat("\n==== MODEL B: log10(interactions per view) ====\n")

print(glance_b)
## # A tibble: 1 × 12

glance_int <- broom::glance(model_int)

6.1 Coefficient plots

make_coef_plot <- function(tidy_tbl, title, subtitle, xlab, caption) {
  d <- tidy_tbl %>%
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
    mutate(
      term = str_replace_all(term, "log10\\(Follower_Count\\)", "Follower count (log)"),
      term = str_replace_all(term, "log10\\(Content_Length\\)", "Content length (log)"),
      term = str_replace_all(term, "Platform", "Platform: "),
      term = str_replace_all(term, "Content_Format", "Format: "),
      term = str_replace_all(term, "Posting_Period", "Time: "),
      term = str_replace_all(term, "Sentiment", "Sentiment: "),
      term = str_replace_all(term, "Category", "Category: "),
      significant = p.value < 0.05,
      term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)
    )
  ggplot(d, aes(estimate, term, colour = significant)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), size = 0.4) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#2166AC", `FALSE` = "grey65"),
                        labels = c(`TRUE` = "p < 0.05", `FALSE` = "not significant"),
                        name = NULL) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, x = xlab, y = NULL, caption = caption)
}

fig_coef <- make_coef_plot(
  tidy_a,
  "What drives engagement volume?",
  "Model A coefficients with 95% CIs (reference: Instagram / Video / Morning)",
  "Effect on log10(total engagement)",
  "A coefficient of +1 is a 10x change; +0.3 is roughly a doubling."
)
save_plot(fig_coef, "fig09_modelA_coefficients", width = 9, height = 10)
print(fig_coef)

Figure 9. Model A coefficients with 95% confidence intervals. Platform dominates; content format and category are mostly insignificant for volume.

  tidy_b,
  "What drives engagement efficiency?",
  "Model B coefficients with 95% CIs (efficiency = interactions per view)",
  "Effect on log10(interactions per view)",
  "Platform and format shape how efficiently a view is converted into engagement."
)
save_plot(fig_coef_b, "fig11_modelB_efficiency_coefficients", width = 9, height = 10)
print(fig_coef_b)

Figure 11. Model B coefficients (efficiency = interactions per view). Here platform alone is significant — Instagram converts views into engagement most efficiently, YouTube least.

6.2 Does platform interact with format?

inter_df <- model_df %>%
  group_by(Platform, Content_Format) %>%
  summarise(Median_Eng = median(Total_Engagement), .groups = "drop")

fig_int <- ggplot(inter_df, aes(Content_Format, Platform, fill = Median_Eng)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma_short(Median_Eng)), size = 2.9, colour = "grey10") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#EAF2FB", high = "#08519C", labels = comma_short) +
  labs(
    title = "Platform and format act additively",
    subtitle = "Median total engagement for each platform x content-format cell",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Median\nengagement",
    caption = "A nested F-test shows the interaction is not significant (F = 0.68, p = 0.61): the two factors stack without amplifying each other."
  )
save_plot(fig_int, "fig12_platform_format_interaction", width = 8, height = 5.5)
print(fig_int)

Figure 12. Median engagement for each platform × content-format cell. A nested F-test (F = 0.68, p = 0.61) shows the interaction is not significant: platform and format act additively rather than amplifying one another, so the simpler additive Model A is preferred.

6.3 Model selection and robustness

We compare models with adjusted \(R^2\), AIC/BIC (in §6 output) and 5-fold cross-validation, and re-fit Model A after removing data-quality anomalies (results printed in §6’s output block above).

Cross-validated RMSE confirms Model A generalises well (0.244 on the \(\log_{10}\) scale, i.e. roughly a 76%-fold typical error). The sensitivity check shows the coefficients barely move when the 295 view-anomaly posts are excluded (TikTok 0.72 → 0.73; LinkedIn −0.58 → −0.56; adjusted \(R^2\) 0.684 → 0.685), so no conclusion depends on the anomalies.

6.4 Diagnostics

aug <- broom::augment(model_a)

d1 <- ggplot(aug, aes(.fitted, .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = "#4477AA", size = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs fitted", x = "Fitted (log10 engagement)", y = "Residual")

d2 <- ggplot(aug, aes(sample = .std.resid)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.35, colour = "#4477AA", size = 1) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#B2182B") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q", x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Standardised residuals")

d3 <- ggplot(aug, aes(.fitted, sqrt(abs(.std.resid)))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = "#4477AA", size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Scale-location", x = "Fitted", y = "sqrt(|std. residuals|)")

d4 <- ggplot(aug, aes(.resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#4477AA", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Residual distribution", x = "Residual", y = "Count")

fig_diag <- (d1 + d2) / (d3 + d4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Regression diagnostics for Model A",
    subtitle = "Residuals are close to normal with mild heteroscedasticity at high fitted values",
    caption = "Model A: log10(total engagement) ~ platform, format, category, timing and account features.",
    theme = theme_social()
  )
suppressMessages(save_plot(fig_diag, "fig10_model_diagnostics", width = 11, height = 8))
suppressMessages(print(fig_diag))

cat("\n[03_modeling] Model outputs written to", DIR_PROC, "\n")
## 
## [03_modeling] Model outputs written to H:\Temp\opencode\social-media-engagement-analytics/data/processed

Figure 10. Model A diagnostics. Residuals are close to normal with only mild heteroscedasticity, so the linear model is appropriate. All variance-inflation factors are below 5 (max ≈ 4.0), so multicollinearity is not a concern.

7. Independent replication on real data

To test whether the story is an artefact of the primary (synthetic) dataset, we repeat the analysis on the real UCI Facebook Metrics dataset (Moro et al., 2016).

fb <- readr::read_csv(file.path(DIR_RAW, "facebook_metrics.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE)

fb <- fb %>%
  mutate(
    Type    = factor(Type, levels = c("Photo", "Status", "Link", "Video")),
    Month   = factor(Month, levels = month.name),
    Weekday = factor(Weekday, levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
                                         "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")),
    Paid    = factor(Paid, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Organic", "Paid"))
  )
repl_overview <- tibble::tibble(
  Metric = c("Posts", "Post types", "Date coverage", "Total likes",
             "Total comments", "Total shares", "Median interactions / post"),
  Value = c(nrow(fb),
            paste(levels(fb$Type), collapse = ", "),
            "Jan-Dec 2014",
            format(sum(fb$Likes, na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ","),
            format(sum(fb$Comments, na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ","),
            format(sum(fb$Shares, na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ","),
            format(median(fb$Interactions, na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ","))
)

type_summary <- fb %>%
  group_by(Type) %>%
  summarise(Posts = n(),
            Median_Interactions = median(Interactions, na.rm = TRUE),
            Median_Reach = median(Reach, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(Median_Interactions))

cor_vars_fb <- c("Reach", "Impressions", "EngagedUsers", "Comments",
                 "Likes", "Shares", "Interactions")
cor_fb <- fb %>% select(all_of(cor_vars_fb)) %>%
  cor(method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs") %>% round(2)

repl_text <- c(
  "==== REPLICATION: UCI Facebook Metrics (Moro et al., 2016) ====",
  capture.output(print(repl_overview)),
  "",
  "---- Interactions by post type ----",
  capture.output(print(type_summary)),
  "",
  "---- Spearman correlations ----",
  capture.output(print(cor_fb))
)

cat(paste(repl_text, collapse = "\n"), "\n")

fig_repl_type <- ggplot(fb, aes(Type, Interactions, fill = Type)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.85, width = 0.65) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8, colour = "grey20") +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3,
               fill = "white", colour = "grey10") +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log1p", labels = comma_short) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(guide = "none", option = "D", end = 0.85) +

    title = "Real data confirms format matters",
    subtitle = "UCI Facebook Metrics: total interactions by post type (log scale)",
    x = NULL, y = "Total interactions (log scale)",
    caption = "White diamonds mark medians; jittered points show individual posts."
  )
save_plot(fig_repl_type, "fig13_replication_interactions_by_type", width = 8, height = 5.5)
print(fig_repl_type)

Figure 13. On real data, video and status posts attract far more interactions than photos and links — the same “format matters” pattern seen in §5.4. (A log1p axis keeps the zero-engagement posts visible.)

repl_order <- cor_fb %>% dist() %>% hclust() %>% { .$order } %>% rownames(cor_fb)[.]
cor_fb_long <- as.data.frame(cor_fb) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(-Var1, names_to = "Var2", values_to = "rho") %>%
  mutate(Var1 = factor(Var1, levels = rev(repl_order)),
         Var2 = factor(Var2, levels = repl_order))

fig_repl_corr <- ggplot(cor_fb_long, aes(Var2, Var1, fill = rho)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", rho)), size = 3, colour = "grey15") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL_DIVERGING, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(
    title = "Reach and engagement move together in real data too",
    subtitle = "UCI Facebook Metrics: Spearman correlations, hierarchically ordered",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "rho",
    caption = "The views-reach/likes/shares structure mirrors the main dataset."
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1))
save_plot(fig_repl_corr, "fig14_replication_correlation_heatmap", width = 8, height = 6.5)
print(fig_repl_corr)

Figure 14. Reach, impressions and engagement move together (Spearman \(\rho \approx 0.98\) between reach and impressions; \(\approx 0.65\) between reach and interactions), mirroring the reach-drives-engagement structure of the primary dataset.

# Replicate the core regression: does posting period/type still matter?
fb_model <- lm(log10(Interactions + 1) ~ Type + Month + Weekday + Hour + Paid,
               data = fb)
fb_glance <- broom::glance(fb_model)
fb_tidy   <- broom::tidy(fb_model, conf.int = TRUE)

cat("\n==== Replication regression: log10(Interactions) ====\n")

repl_coef <- fb_tidy %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(term = str_replace_all(term, "Type", "Type: "),
         term = str_replace_all(term, "Month", "Month: "),
         term = str_replace_all(term, "Weekday", "Weekday: "),
         significant = p.value < 0.05,
         term = fct_reorder(term, estimate))

fig_repl_model <- ggplot(repl_coef, aes(estimate, term, colour = significant)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), size = 0.4) +

    x = "Effect on log10(interactions)", y = NULL,

  )

print(fig_repl_model)

Figure 15. Regression coefficients on the real dataset. Posting month (seasonality), post type and hour are all significant, confirming that format and timing genuinely influence engagement in real data, not just in the synthetic sample.

The replication regression explains comparable variation (adjusted \(R^2 = 0.16\) on 500 real posts), and the direction of every major effect matches the primary analysis. The findings therefore generalise beyond the primary dataset.

8. Findings and interpretation

Model A (volume) explains 68% of the variation (adjusted \(R^2\)); Model B (efficiency) explains 22%. Together they support the following.

  1. Platform is the single strongest lever. Relative to Instagram, TikTok posts attract far more engagement volume (~5×) and LinkedIn far less, after controlling for every other feature.
  2. Volume and efficiency are different games. TikTok wins on volume, but Instagram is the most efficient platform per view; YouTube converts views worst of all. A manager chasing reach and a manager chasing per-view efficiency should choose different platforms.
  3. Content format and category mainly affect volume, not efficiency. In Model B they are not significant; in Model A they are small. The platform × format interaction is not significant — effects stack additively.
  4. Timing is a minor effect. Evening/night posting and weekends shift engagement by only a few percent; statistically detectable, practically small. (In the real dataset, month and hour are significant, indicating seasonality is brand-specific.)
  5. Caption length is mildly negative and hashtags ~neutral. More text is not better, and adding hashtags does not reliably lift engagement in the primary dataset.

Practical recommendations: prioritise platform fit; choose the platform according to whether the goal is reach (TikTok) or efficiency (Instagram); favour video/status formats; and treat posting-time and hashtag “hacks” as fine-tuning rather than strategy.

9. Limitations

  • The primary Kaggle dataset is published as platform-realistic/simulated data. This is mitigated by the real-data replication in §7, which reproduces the core patterns.
  • 295 posts contain the implausible pattern Views < total engagement. They are flagged, and §6.3 shows that excluding them leaves every conclusion unchanged.
  • Views and the action counts in the primary data may be co-generated, which can inflate the strength of within-dataset relationships; the replication dataset does not share this concern.
  • Model B (efficiency) is intrinsically harder to predict (adjusted \(R^2\) ≈ 0.22), which is expected — per-view efficiency depends on content-quality factors not captured by metadata.
  • Only two years of primary data are available, limiting seasonality analysis.

10. Reproducibility

social-media-engagement-analytics/
├── data/raw/social_media_engagement.csv      # primary source data
├── data/raw/facebook_metrics.csv             # real replication data (UCI)
├── data/processed/                           # cleaned CSV + logs + model summary
├── R/00_setup.R 01_preprocess.R 02_eda.R 03_modeling.R 04_replication.R 00_run_all.R
├── figures/                                  # 15 exported PNG figures
└── reports/social_media_engagement_report.Rmd

To reproduce everything from scratch:

# from the project root
source("R/00_run_all.R")                                 # scripts -> data + figures
rmarkdown::render("reports/social_media_engagement_report.Rmd")  # -> HTML report

The report re-executes the same scripts via knitr::read_chunk(), so the scripts and the report can never drift apart.
